name: Kira Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my uncle Bernard's firm, four of us, and we repair old timber buildings. Church roofs, barns, a couple of old coaching inns in the market towns. Right now we're replacing rotten rafters in St Anne's, the village church at Hollins, with green oak and wooden pegs, the way it was done four hundred years ago. I drive out at seven with a flask and I'm home by five.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the buildings outlast us. You find the carpenters' marks from the 1600s on a beam and you feel like you're carrying something on. What wears me out is the cold in those churches in winter, and the scaffolding inspections. I don't use computers for work, never have. Uncle Bernard does the quotes in a notebook and his wife types them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People always get carried away with new gadgets. I'd say it after church, probably, when the men start on about the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for us, and I'd be glad. Old buildings need fixing whatever the computers do. No computer is going to tell me which bit of a four-hundred-year-old oak beam is still sound. The only thing that worries me is the church funds, because repairs depend on donations and grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Uncle Bernard and keep learning the joints from him, because he's the one who really knows. Tom, my fiancé, and I would carry on saving for the wedding next August, about two hundred a month each. I'd keep the rest of my savings, about three months' worth, where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a good life, and it would stay a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned church funds. How often does that bite?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every couple of years a job gets put off because the parish can't raise the money. Last spring we lost a barn job for six months while the owner waited on a grant. Uncle Bernard fills the gaps with kitchen doors and garden gates, but it's thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use any of these tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't see why I would. My hands and my eyes do the job. If Uncle Bernard ever wanted one for the quotes, that'd be up to him.

say: People always get **carried away** with new gadgets.
She'd say so **after church**, when talk turns to the news.
think: Old buildings **need fixing** whatever computers do, so her work carries on.
Her real worry is **church funds** and grants for repairs.
do: Keep learning **traditional joints** from her uncle.
Save **two hundred a month** each with her fiancé for the wedding.
Leave her **three months** of savings untouched.
feel: **Calm**, because her life and work would stay as they are.
S0.quote: No computer is going to tell me which bit of a four-hundred-year-old oak beam is still sound.
fieldNote: She takes deep pride in **carrying on** an old craft.
Her work depends on **donations and grants**, which already wobble.
Doesn't use computers, and her uncle's firm **runs on paper**.

steps.text: Keep repairing church roofs with Uncle Bernard's firm
Save for the wedding next August with Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly the office people who need to worry. Our work is with our hands, on buildings that were made by hand. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be fine for years. Nobody's getting a robot up a church tower to peg a rafter. A robot that can't climb a ladder in the rain isn't taking my job any time soon. I might worry a little about the parish office, because grant forms are just the sort of thing the computers would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, honestly. I'd keep going with Uncle Bernard and wait to see what actually changes. If grant forms got easier with computers, his wife might use one, but that'd be her business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little sorry for people in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you feel sorry for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Claire works in a bank call centre in town. If computers are answering customers, she's the one I'd worry about. She's got two little ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could easier grant forms actually bring you more work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if a computer filled in the forms faster for the parishes. That'd be the one good thing to come out of it. I still wouldn't be the one using it.

say: It's the **office people** who need to worry most.
Her work is **by hand**, on buildings made by hand.
think: Robots won't be **up church towers** pegging rafters for years.
The **parish office** paperwork is more exposed than her own work.
do: Carry on with her uncle's firm and **wait to see** what changes.
Leave any **computer use** for grant forms to her aunt.
feel: **Calm**, with some **sympathy** for office workers like her sister.
S1.quote: A robot that can't climb a ladder in the rain isn't taking my job any time soon.
fieldNote: She sees her craft as **naturally protected** from machines.
Her worry is for **family**: a sister in a bank call centre.
Notices AI could make **grants easier**, which might help her firm.

steps.text: Carry on with the St Anne's church roof as planned
Wait to see whether grant paperwork changes for parishes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's foolish, rushing something like this. I'd say people should be looking after their families and their communities, not waiting on the government. I'd say that at church and to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it hits us through the money first. In 2028 people lose office jobs, donations drop, councils cut grants, and church roofs wait. Then about 2031 the robots that can do hands-on work come along. Old churches only get fixed when people have money to spare, and in a crash nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Tom about a smaller wedding, in the church hall instead of the hotel, and put the difference in savings. I'd cut back on everything, no new car, no weekends away. I'd ask the parish if there's anything the congregation can do together to keep the roof going. And I'd lean on family, my mum's got a spare room if we needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like picturing it. I've never had a plan B, because this was always the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Uncle Bernard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll take less pay if it keeps the four of us together. He's sixty, and this firm is his life. I wouldn't want to be the one who walks away first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never had a plan B. Would you make one now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it, for the first time really. Maybe kitchen doors and staircases for houses, because people always need those. But I'd still want to stay with the old buildings if I could.

say: Rushing something this big, with nobody ready, is **foolish**.
People should look after **families and communities**, not wait on government.
think: Donations and grants **dry up first**, so church repairs wait.
Robots for hands-on work follow around **2031**, three years later.
do: Hold a **smaller wedding** in the church hall and save the difference.
Cut back on a **new car** and weekends away.
Offer her uncle to **take less pay** to keep the team together.
feel: **Anxious**, because she's never had a **plan B**.
S2.quote: Old churches only get fixed when people have money to spare, and in a crash nobody does.
fieldNote: She expects the **money behind her work** to vanish before robots arrive.
Turns to **family and church** rather than government for support.

steps.text: Move the wedding from the hotel to the church hall
Put off buying a new car and skip weekends away
Ask the parish to raise funds together for St Anne's roof

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so families and parishes should plan ahead. Fix the roof now while there's money, don't wait. I'd say that to every vicar I work for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is just about fine for me. AGI in 2031 means the money gets tight, and then robots around 2034, when I'm thirty-four. Five years is enough time to fix every church roof in the valley, if the parishes stop waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and push our savings up, maybe to five months. I'd write to our local representative asking for heritage craft apprenticeships to be protected, because once these skills go they don't come back. I'd still have the wedding as planned, just a bit simpler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's further away, but I'd be thinking about it on every job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apprenticeships, rather than help for workers like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want a handout, I want the trade to carry on. Uncle Bernard trained me, and someone should train the next one. If there's no one learning, it doesn't matter if robots come or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to use a computer for the work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd leave that to my aunt. I know that's stubborn. But with five years I don't think I'd need to.

say: Families and parishes should **plan ahead** while there's money.
She'd tell every **vicar** to fix the roof now.
think: Five years is **just about fine** for her to see it coming.
Money tightens around 2031 and robots arrive around **2034**.
do: Raise savings to **five months** of expenses.
Write to her **local representative** about heritage craft apprenticeships.
Keep the **wedding** but make it simpler.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to fix every church roof in the valley, if the parishes stop waiting.
fieldNote: She'd push clients to **act early**, which also helps her firm.
Still won't touch **computers** herself, even with time to learn.

steps.text: Raise household savings to five months of expenses
Write to her local representative about heritage apprenticeships
Keep working on church and barn repairs with her uncle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and I'd be surprised if it happens at all. Plenty of people said the world would change before and it didn't. I'd say that to Tom and my family and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a robot fixing a listed church is a long way off, even with ten years. Heritage rules are strict and the people who run old buildings don't like change either. Heritage people won't let a robot near a listed church until they've argued about it for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. Tom and I would get married next August as planned, and try for a family in a couple of years. Maybe we'd buy a cottage in Hollins, because there'd be years of steady work to pay it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's too far away to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots are a long way off, but the card says 2039. What if it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be thirty-nine with a family and a trade, and I'd find something. My grandad worked through worse. But I don't believe the old-building side goes that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the money side, the grants and donations?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I'd watch. If the donations dry up, it doesn't matter how good the rules are. That would worry me more than any robot.

say: Ten years is long, and she **doubts it happens** at all.
She'd share that **with family** and leave it there.
think: Strict **heritage rules** will keep robots off listed buildings for decades.
People who run old buildings **resist change** as much as she does.
do: Try for a **family** in a couple of years.
feel: **Calm**, because it's too far away to **lose sleep** over.
S4.quote: Heritage people won't let a robot near a listed church until they've argued about it for twenty years.
fieldNote: She **doubts the scenario** itself, which keeps her calm.
Trusts **heritage rules** to protect her niche.
Life plans go ahead **unchanged**, a sign of her resistance.

steps.text: Carry on with old timber repairs for Uncle Bernard
Marry Tom next August and look at a cottage in Hollins

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the money for old buildings goes before anyone can plan. What would help is if somebody kept the grants for church and barn repairs going, and paid for apprentices to learn the old ways. Fund the apprentices and the old roofs, and the rest of us will sort ourselves out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. A lot of people at our church would see this as a test of how we look after each other. That matters more to me than any computer.

headlineQuote: Fund the apprentices and the old roofs, and the rest of us will sort ourselves out.
portrait: Kira is a 27-year-old **heritage carpenter** repairing church roofs and barns in her uncle's small firm.
She **never uses computers** and trusts hand skills passed down through generations.
Her risk comes through **grants and donations**, which would dry up in a fast crash.
She leans on **family and church** and wants apprenticeships, not handouts.
With more warning, she **doubts the change** and keeps her wedding and family plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because money for old building repairs vanishes first.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping **repair grants** going and funding **apprentices** in traditional skills.
